title: The grace before meals
hookLine: the verse many families say before dinner, and a list of a dozen ways to make an offering

lines: THE FOOD IS SERVED. EVERYONE WAITS.
A VERSE AT THE DINNER TABLE.
cards: In some Hindu homes, and in some school dining halls in India, the food is served, everyone waits, and a short Sanskrit verse is chanted before anyone eats.
Some children learn it by ear long before they know what it means. Brahmarpanam, it begins. It's a grace before meals, and it comes from Gita chapter four, verse twenty-four.
The surprise is what it says. It doesn't thank anyone for the food. It says the food, the eater, the fire and the offering are all one thing.
So how did a verse about fire end up at the dinner table?

teach.h: THE FIRE, THE GHEE, THE PRIEST.
teach.b: In the old Vedic sacrifice, the yajna, a priest pours ghee into a fire, and the fire carries the offering to the gods. Verse twenty-four turns that scene inside out. The act of offering is Brahman.
The offering is Brahman, poured by Brahman into the fire, which is Brahman. And the one who sees Brahman in the action reaches Brahman. Every part of the ritual is the same reality.

So when families chant it over a plate of rice, the meal becomes the fire, the eating becomes the offering. Then Krishna lists the ways people sacrifice, and the list keeps widening. Some offer to the gods.
Some offer their senses into the fire of self-control. Some offer their wealth, or austerity, or yoga, or the study of scripture.

teach.h: EVEN BREATH CAN BE AN OFFERING.
teach.b: Some offer the in-breath into the out-breath, and the out-breath into the in-breath. Even breathing can be a sacrifice. Then verse thirty-three ranks them.
Better than any offering of things, Krishna says, is the offering of knowledge, because all action ends in knowledge. The fire has moved inside. What burns now isn't ghee; it's ignorance.
A few verses later he says it outright: as a blazing fire turns wood to ash, the fire of knowledge turns karma to ash. Seeing clearly is itself the offering, and the seeing burns.

how: Some Hindu families, schools and ashrams chant Gita 4.24 (brahmarpanam) as a grace before meals; the idea of offering breath, study and work as yajna shapes daily practice for some.

o: an offering, once poured into a fire
a prayer of thanks before a meal

games.q: what's inside the fire — tap the pairs.

s: in the Gita, sacrifice only means rituals with fire
Krishna's list includes self-control, wealth, study, yoga and even the breath.
the brahmarpanam verse is used as a grace before meals
some families and schools chant Gita 4.24 before eating.
Krishna says an offering of things beats an offering of knowledge
verse 33 says the reverse: knowledge is higher, since all action ends in it.

games.q: Krishna lists many kinds of offering: to the gods, of wealth, of study, of the breath. which does he call the highest?
games.why: knowledge. verse 33: all action culminates in knowledge, so the offering of knowledge is higher than any offering of things.

practice: Verse twenty-nine makes breathing an offering.

Breathe in slowly and think, this is given; breathe out and think, this is given back, with nothing to fix and nothing to earn, and when your mind wanders, come back to the next breath. If you pray, you can offer the breath to God.

wordCard.voice: Yajna. Sacrifice, offering: the old fire ritual moved inward. Seeing clearly is the highest offering, and the fire it lights burns karma.

orig.note: Sanskrit: yajna, sacrifice or offering; the fire ritual of the Vedas, which the Gita widens to all of life.

carryVoice: Your line: knowledge burns karma. Even a plate of rice can be an offering. That's day one hundred seventy-three.
